name: Pearl
lede: Pearl is the pale, cool grey of the gem's body color, though real pearls range from white to black, and a pearl's glow comes from layered light, not from pigment.

sections.title: A grey that is really a range
sections.body:
The swatch is a light, slightly greenish grey. Our library lists it as Pearl from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color, which gives 1604 as the first recorded use of the word as a color, and ISCC-NBS calls the nearest block a light greenish gray, 5.0 units away [14]. St Clair's glossary describes pearl more loosely, as a very pale lilac-grey [8].

Neither description is wrong, because a pearl has no single color. Finlay lists the colors that pearls come in as pure white, champagne, apricot, bronze, pink, lavender, grey and black, and very rarely green [1]. The swatch is therefore the grey end of a gem that runs almost the whole range, and it stands in for the cool, quiet one [1][14]. Near it in the library are [[pearl-grey]], [[pearl-beige]], [[pearl-violet]] and [[warm-silver]] [14].

sections.title: Why a pearl is not a flat color
sections.body:
Part of what we call pearl is not pigment. Livingstone counts pearls among the things whose colors come from interference, where light bounces between thin layers and the hue shifts with the angle of view [7]. Signac, she notes, compared his divided colors with a pearl for that reason, since both change as you move [7]. A flat grey swatch can only ever suggest this, which is why dictionaries add words for it: Paterson defines *mother of pearl* as the iridescent color of the shell's nacreous surface, and *margaric* as having the luster of pearl [9].

Finlay adds that buyers judge a pearl on four things, its size, its color, its "orient", meaning the way it shimmers and reflects light, and its shape [1]. Orient usually depends on how many layers of nacre there are [1]. The color named pearl is therefore the body color without the orient, and the gem's full effect needs both [1][7].

sections.title: Pearls of the river
sections.body:
Finlay's account of Scottish pearl fishers shows how local pearl color can be [1]. By his report, rose-pink pearls came from Scotland, black pearls from Ennerdale in Cumbria and white ones from Ireland, and all three were exported across Europe for centuries [1]. A fisherman he met said the pearls of the River Oykel were a sweet rose pink and always the most valuable [1]. The same fisherman credited the peat in the water for the strong colors and added that the pearls of Lapland, a land without peat, run grey [1]. That explanation is one man's belief, so treat it as folk knowledge until a gemologist confirms it [1].

An old English word for a pearl was *union*, from the Latin *unio*, meaning unique [1]. Each river, in a fisher's boast, leaves its own signature on its pearls [1].

sections.title: Rome, Britain and a drink
sections.body:
In Finlay's retelling of Suetonius, Julius Caesar's invasion of Britain was partly about its river pearls [1]. Caesar is reported to have restricted pearls to aristocrats and to have bought one for Servilia at sixty thousand gold pieces [1]. Pearls were linked to Venus, and a string of them was a sign of unimaginable wealth when few people owned even one [1]. None of this is certain, because Finlay passes on the ancient authors' reports, and a reader should hear them as such [1].

The best-known pearl story is Cleopatra's [1]. Pliny tells how she and Mark Antony competed to give the most lavish dinner, and how she won by dissolving a pearl from her earring in vinegar and drinking it [1]. Finlay doubts that it happened that way, and one scholar he cites suggests she swallowed the pearl whole [1]. When Finlay left a natural pearl in strong vinegar, it showed no change for hours, split in half after a day, and was soft mush after thirty-two days [1]. The story is more likely moralizing than reporting [1].

The Renaissance painter's handbook took up the joke [5][6]. Alberti wrote that painters would be properly sparing with white and black if those pigments were made from the pearls Cleopatra dissolved in vinegar [5][6].

sections.title: Pearl white, the pigment that was not
sections.body:
The name also belonged to painters. Pearl white, in French *blanc de perle*, was the name for bismuth white, a basic bismuth nitrate or chloride [4]. The *Pigment Compendium* notes that Tingry, in 1830, called bismuth white from Cornwall pearl white, and that Field in 1835, with his editor Salter in 1869, treated bismuth nitrate under the same name [4]. The book suggests that the names became conflated because real pearls had once been among the materials used for "magisteries", the residues precipitated from acid solutions, though it frames this as a guess [4].

Real pearl did turn up in whites elsewhere. Finlay lists the shell paints of Japanese and Chinese painting as made from seashells, eggshells, oysters and chalk, and even from pearls, though those painters often thought the best white was the unpainted paper [10].

sections.title: A white for the top of the hierarchy
sections.body:
In the medieval order of precious things, Pastoureau reports, pearls ranked above gemstones, gold, ivory, sable and silk [11]. The Latin name for the pearl, *margarita*, gave Margaret its prestige, and white in general was assigned the diamond or pearl among stones [11]. Dyers had their own ladder: Balfour-Paul quotes eighteenth-century dyers' thirteen shades of blue, which start with milk-blue and pearl-blue and end at navy [12]. The ladder ran from the palest to the deepest [12].

In nineteenth-century mourning, Finlay writes, Queen Victoria was wearing "white jewelry", mostly pearls and diamonds, in later widowhood, which royal families still treat as acceptable at any stage of mourning [1].

sections.title: Making pearls: Linnaeus to Mikimoto
sections.body:
The pearl business changed in the early twentieth century. Linnaeus had experimented with a way to make pearls in mussels in 1758, and his method was thought lost until his papers were found in 1901 [1]. In 1884 the Frenchman Bouchon-Brandely got a handful of pearls out of black-lipped oysters in Tahiti, and in 1890 William Saville Kent produced a spherical cultured pearl in New South Wales, though he kept the method secret [1].

Kokichi Mikimoto found five round pearls in 1905 after a red tide killed his oysters, and these taught him where to place the nucleus [1]. When he sent pearls to London in 1919, Finlay writes, jewelers in Europe and America panicked, because the cultured pearls were as good as natural ones and often better [1]. Their stocks of natural pearls were worth a vast amount [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Pearl is far more common in painting than most colors of its kind. Counting a painting when the color covers at least 1 per cent of the canvas, it appears in 793 of 23,781 paintings, 3.33 per cent, as photographed [13]. That is more common than 84 per cent of the named colors [13]. Within a painting it most often plays a light, in 54 per cent of the 542 paintings that the lightness-rank lens catches, so varnish cannot fake the role [13].

It peaks in the 1900s: 4.1 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 69 in all, 1.8 times the rate its museums would predict [13]. The most devoted painter is Eugène Boudin, with 10 of his 33 works here, 8.7 times the baseline of their museums; [[painter:henri-matisse|Matisse]] also appears in 10 of 50 [13]. Among movements, Impressionism holds it in 12 of 140 paintings, at 2.7 times the baseline [13]. It tends to share canvases with Battleship Grey and Deep Neutral Grey [13].

The caveat is the usual one: photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [13]. The first matching painting in the archive is dated 1164, long before the name's earliest record in our sources, 1930, so the hue was older than the word [13][14]. For the gem itself, see [[gem:pearl|pearl]], and for the nearest of the iridescent family, [[gem:moonstone|moonstone]] and [[gem:opal|opal]].
